name: Venancio Chávez
equipment: Leather duster, fine black broadcloth, over a brocade waistcoat with silver buttons
Pocket revolver (Colt, .32), 5 rounds loaded, in his waistcoat
Boot knife, in his left boot, and a second in his sleeve that he denies
A Spanish deck for monte, worn soft, and an English deck for the Anglos, marked
The keys to La Golondrina, its back room and its strongbox
A ledger, in his head, of every vote on the plaza and what it has cost in twenty years
A letter from Fenton Rusk on Paragon Mercantile paper, about Venancio's $600 note, which he keeps folded in his waistcoat and has not shown to anyone
A guitar, which he plays well and only after midnight
Horse: Don Cristóbal, a fat, elegant black gelding with a silver-mounted bridle
features: Both Sides of the River (Borderlands origin: speaks Spanish and English natively; knows everyone in every plaza of the Rio Abajo or knows their cousin; advantage on Persuasion and Insight checks with border people of either side)

Read the Table (Gambler: proficiency doubled for Gambling and Insight; once per short rest, after a minute of watching or talking to someone, learns one thing they are hiding; always knows whether a game is honest)

Ace in the Hole (Gambler: once per turn, +2d6 damage with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm when he has advantage, when another enemy of the target is within 5 ft, or when the target believed a lie he told it in the last minute; not part of the damage on his sheet)
Lady Luck (Gambler, 2nd level: 4 luck points per long rest; spend one to roll an extra d20 on an attack, check or save and choose, or to make a creature within 30 ft reroll an attack against him)

Sleeve Gun (Gambler, 2nd level: draws a concealable weapon as a bonus action unseen by anyone not watching his hands; advantage on Sleight of Hand to carry one past a search; can Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action)
Game: Faro Dealer (Gambler, 3rd level: runs a monte bank at La Golondrina, earning 1d6 x 5 dollars a night; the house always knows who is winning, who is drinking and who is broke)

Behind the Bar (Saloon Keeper background: in any cantina or saloon he gets the last week's gossip from the bartender in one drink; knows who drinks on credit, who wins at monte, who has been asking about whom and who is about to start a fight; saloon keepers and musicians treat him as one of the trade)

personality.traits: I am charming to everyone and honest with almost no one, and I never forget a name, a face or a debt. I dress better than the patrón and drink less than you think. I laugh at my own jokes, because somebody has to.
personality.ideals: Politics is favours. A man who gives the plaza a drink, a dollar and a job for his son has earned its vote, and a man who has not has no business asking for it. But a man who counts wrong is a thief.
personality.bonds: La Golondrina, which my father built and I have kept for twenty years. The plaza, which I have delivered at every election since 1861 and will deliver this time. My daughter Rosario, who is at the convent school in Santa Fe and thinks her father is a respectable businessman.
personality.flaws: I owe the Company $600, and it has offered to forgive it if I steal sixty votes. I have bought votes all my life and never once thought it was a sin. Now I do not know what I think.

appearance: A plump, elegant, moustached man of forty-five with silver at his temples, heavy-lidded clever eyes, rings on three fingers and a voice like warm oil. Black broadcloth, a brocade waistcoat with silver buttons, a flat black hat with a silver band, and boots polished every morning.
backstory: Venancio Chávez was born in 1836 on the plaza of Santa Teresita, the son of a muleteer who saved enough from the Chihuahua trade to build a cantina, and he has stood behind its bar since he was twelve. He has run La Golondrina since 1859, its monte bank since 1861, and the plaza's vote since the first territorial election he can remember, for whichever party the plaza favoured that year. He knows every family, every debt, every feud and every vote on the plaza, and in twenty years he has never lost his precinct. He is the People's party's precinct boss and one of the three judges of election at the plaza. In the bad winter of 1880 he borrowed $600 from the Paragon Mercantile to keep the cantina open, and in June the Company bought his note. On 5 July a friendly letter came from Fenton Rusk: if the Progress ticket carries the plaza by sixty votes more than the honest count, the note will be torn up; if not, it will be called on 15 July. He has told no one, and he has not decided. (Companion. Hooks: the plaza's count; Rusk's letter; who the repeaters are, because he knows the type.)

dmNotes.roleplaying: Venancio is the plaza's machine: charming, corrupt in the ordinary way of every territorial politician, and suddenly faced with corruption of a different kind. Use him as the party's guide to how the election really works. He can tell them every precinct's likely vote within ten (campaignRules, The Vote), which repeaters are repeaters, and how a count is stolen. His arc is the plaza count on election night (st-scenario-003). Don't make him a villain or a saint. He bought votes with whiskey for twenty years and is proud of it, and he finds he cannot make himself do this. Let the party talk to him as a friend at the monte table, not preach at him.
dmNotes.voice: Warm, amused, fluent and flowery in both languages, full of proverbs he half invents. Calls everyone "amigo" or "señora" and the Company "los señores de Paragon" with exquisite contempt. Goes very quiet and plain when he is frightened, which is the tell.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: keep La Golondrina. Secondary: keep his precinct and his name. Tertiary: his daughter's good opinion, which he would lose if she ever knew about either the old votes or the new offer.
dmNotes.secrets: Rusk's letter in his waistcoat, offering to forgive the $600 note for a false count of sixty votes on the plaza, in Rusk's own hand. It is a crime and it is evidence. He gives it to someone who frees him from the note, or who simply makes him feel he does not have to do it (st-scenario-003, Venancio's Note). He also knows, from twenty years of elections, that the Company's tickets will be printed to look like the People's, because that is what he would do. He will say so if asked, and then be ashamed of how he knows.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: delighted, flattering, useful, and watching their hands. Toward Celestino: thinks him a fine speaker and no politician. Toward Don Fermín: old respect and old resentment. Toward Rusk: fear, and contempt for a man who cannot win honestly even by Venancio's standards. Toward Theodora Quayle, if played: professional admiration; he will want her to deal faro at La Golondrina, and she will be tempted.
